summary: This document defines a collection of YANG definitions for configuring SNMP engines.

plainLanguage.summary: YANG is a language for describing device settings. This RFC uses it to describe the settings for the older monitoring system called SNMP.

questions: what is the yang data model for snmp
how to configure snmp with netconf
subtitle: A YANG model that lets NETCONF configure SNMP engines, targets, users and access rules.

tldr.problem: SNMP agents are traditionally configured through SNMP MIB tables, which does not fit deployments that run SNMP read-only and manage devices with NETCONF.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the ietf-snmp YANG module, split into submodules that mirror the SNMP configuration MIBs, plus a module that maps X.509 certificates to names. Most nodes map 1-1 to a MIB object.
tldr.outcome: Operators can configure an SNMP engine over NETCONF in a hierarchical model, while implementations can still allow SNMP write access if they handle datastore persistence carefully.

today: RFC 7407 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the YANG definition for configuring SNMP engines described here.

sections.title: Why SNMP Needs a YANG Model
sections.content:
RFC 7407 defines a YANG data model for configuring SNMP engines. It is consistent with the MIB modules that define SNMP's architecture, message processing, applications, security models and transport models, but it uses YANG's ability to express hierarchical configuration.

The model was designed for deployments where SNMP runs in read-only mode and the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) configures the SNMP agent. It still allows implementations that accept writes both over SNMP and over NETCONF, so existing SNMP management applications keep working.

It models configuration only. Operational state is not modeled; it stays reachable through SNMP itself, or through NETCONF using the read-only YANG translation of the MIB modules defined in RFC 6643. The RFC also defines a separate YANG module that maps an X.509 certificate to a name.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a toy with a settings dial that only worked one old way. This RFC adds a new, tidy control panel so grown-ups can set the toy up in one standard way.

sections.title: How the Model Is Organized
sections.content:
To keep SNMP's modularity, the configuration model is a set of YANG submodules that all share one module namespace, ietf-snmp. A new SNMP feature can add its own configuration without adding another namespace.

The submodule ietf-snmp-common defines common typedefs and the top-level container snmp. Every other submodule hangs its configuration under that container: engine, target, notification, proxy, community, VACM, USM, TSM, TLS and SSH.

Most YANG nodes map 1-1 to a MIB object, and a reference statement names the object. When the mapping is not simple, the description statement explains it. Two SNMP conventions are deliberately absent: the StorageType columns (in NETCONF the datastore decides persistence) and the RowStatus columns (NETCONF handles creation and deletion).
sections.plainLanguage: The settings form is split into small pages, one for each topic, but they all live in the same binder. Things the old form needed only for its own paperwork are left off.

sections.title: Engine, Targets and Notifications
sections.content:
The engine submodule configures the engine itself: an enabled switch, a listen list of transport endpoints (SNMP over UDP is defined here), a version container that enables or disables v1, v2c and v3, an engine-id and enable-authen-traps.

The target submodule corresponds to SNMP-TARGET-MIB. A target list entry maps to an snmpTargetAddrEntry and names a transport address, tags, a timeout and retries. A target-params list entry maps to an snmpTargetParamsEntry and holds a params choice that security-model submodules extend.

The notification submodule adds the notify and notify-filter-profile lists. The sparse MIB relationship between target parameters and filter profiles becomes a leafref named notify-filter-profile. The proxy submodule adds a proxy list and a proxy feature for servers that can act as an SNMP proxy.
sections.plainLanguage: One page says whether the SNMP helper is switched on and where it listens. Other pages say who it should send news to and which kinds of news to send.

sections.title: Security, Access Control and Certificates
sections.content:
Each SNMP security model gets its own submodule. community configures the Community-based Security Model used by SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c; choosing the v1 or v2c case implies a security level of noAuthNoPriv. usm configures the User-based Security Model, with a list of local users and a nested list of remote users per engine ID, each with optional auth (md5 or sha) and priv (des or aes) keys.

The vacm submodule configures View-based Access Control. Groups hold member and access sublists, and views use compact include and exclude leaf-lists of subtrees. The tsm submodule covers the Transport Security Model, and ietf-snmp-tls and ietf-snmp-ssh add TLS, DTLS and SSH transports for both listening endpoints and targets.

The TLS submodule also holds a cert-to-name list. The separate ietf-x509-cert-to-name module defines the identities, such as specified, san-rfc822-name, san-dns-name and san-ip-address, that say how a name is derived from a certificate. The algorithm was first defined in RFC 6353.
sections.plainLanguage: There are pages for the different ways to prove who you are and for deciding who may see or change what. One page also explains how to turn the name on an ID card into a user name.

sections.title: Implementation Guidelines
sections.content:
Supporting both NETCONF and SNMP access to the same data is hard because their persistence models differ. NETCONF has up to three datastores (running, candidate, startup), while SNMP rows carry StorageType and RowStatus. The RFC does not recommend one solution; it describes the challenges.

For read-only SNMP access, if a device implements only :writable-running, the contents of running map directly to SNMP rows with nonVolatile storage. If the device implements :startup, an entry present in running but not in startup should be volatile, and an entry only in startup should not appear in the default SNMP context.

For read-write SNMP access, only rows with an active RowStatus should be stored in a configuration datastore. With :startup, nonVolatile rows must be copied into startup as well as running. Implementations that change spin-lock-protected objects through NETCONF should increment the spin lock objects so cooperating SNMP managers can see concurrent changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Two people sharing one notebook must agree on what is a permanent note and what is scribbled in pencil. This part lists the tricky cases rather than picking one rule.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is meant to be accessed over NETCONF, whose mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH, and the NETCONF access control model can restrict users to a subset of operations and content. Writable nodes are sensitive: the RFC lists subtrees such as /snmp/engine, /snmp/target, /snmp/community, /snmp/usm, /snmp/tlstm and /snmp/vacm, and says write access to the security-related ones should go only to the security administrator.

Readable nodes can also be sensitive. The community, usm, tsm, tlstm and vacm subtrees are called out as especially sensitive because they expose the authentication and authorization policy of the engine.

Changes to SNMP access control rules should be atomic, or ordered so access is never temporarily opened. Changes involving an internal delete/create cycle must be protected so that even a power failure right after the delete does not lock the administrator out.

Security administrators must also keep NETCONF and SNMP access rules consistent, so that, for example, community strings do not leak.
sections.plainLanguage: The settings form controls who gets in, so only trusted people should be allowed to change it, and changes must never leave the door briefly unlocked or lock the owner out.

sections.title: Example Configurations
sections.content: Appendix A gives XML instance documents for each area. The engine example configures an SNMP engine listening on UDP port 161 on IPv4 and IPv6 endpoints and accepting SNMPv2c and SNMPv3 messages. Other examples cover a community mapping, USM users, targets and notifications, a proxy, VACM, and TLS transport configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: At the back there are filled-in sample forms, so you can see what a finished settings page looks like.
